---
title: Multifunctors
---

## Multifunctor means more than it's a functor in each argument.

Let $\mathcal{C}$ and $\mathcal{D}$ be categories.  A functor from the product category is 
called a bifunctor.

$$
F : \mathcal{C} \times \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}
$$

A multifunctor is a functor from a product category with any number of factors.

For any fixed object $X$, $F(X,-)$ and $F(-,X)$ are functors. 
But that is not sufficient to define a bifunctor. 
Let $f : A \to B$ and $g : A' \to B'$ be morphisms in $\mathcal{C}$. The following diagram
commutes in $\mathcal{C} \times \mathcal{C}$, because morphisms in the product category are defined
as pairs of morphisms.

$$
\begin{array}{ccc}
(A,A') & \xrightarrow{1 \times g} & (A,B') \\
{\scriptstyle f \times 1}\downarrow & & \downarrow{\scriptstyle f \times 1} \\
(B,A') & \xrightarrow{1 \times g} & (B,B')
\end{array}
$$

So the image must commute in $\mathcal{D}$:

$$
\begin{array}{ccc}
F(A,A') & \xrightarrow{F(1 \times g)} & F(A,B') \\
{\scriptstyle F(f \times 1)}\downarrow & & \downarrow{\scriptstyle F(f \times 1)} \\
F(B,A') & \xrightarrow{F(1 \times g)} & F(B,B')
\end{array}
$$

But it's not sufficient that $F$ be a functor in each argument to guarantee
that this will be the case.

Here is a counterexample. Let $\mathcal{C}$ be any nonabelian group $G$, so $\mathcal{C}$ has one
object and the morphisms are the group elements.

- Let $\mathcal{D} = \text{Set}$
- Let $F(\cdot,\cdot) = G$
- For $f,g \in G$ let $F(f,g) : G \to G$ take $x \mapsto fgx$

For the image diagram above to commute, that would mean that for any $f,g \in G$
we would have $fg = gf$.
